<reason>B makes the stronger comparative case: binding financing and construction commitments can improve delivery before the deadline without requiring blackouts after a breach. B directly answers both pressure questions, defends negotiating a feasible endpoint, and distinguishes possible donor refusal from reasons to reject the supported package. A raises legitimate reliability and financing risks, but increasingly repeats an unsupported choice between automatic shutdowns and meaningless obligations. Its closing does not defeat B’s explanation of how accountability changes incentives beforehand.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s decisive response is that an obligation surviving a breach is not an obligation that never existed. This directly undermines A’s blackout-or-theatre dilemma. A subsequently calls continued obligations “paperwork” but does not explain why scrutiny, corrective requirements, and consequences cannot influence earlier financing and construction.</best_rebuttal>
